name: Forty Fathoms, No Bottom
description: A low-budget holographic thriller about a Shelf salvage diver who finds a submerged pre-city structure in the lakebed containing what appears to be an intact pre-Compact data archive — and the escalating interest from multiple corponations in ensuring it never surfaces. Shot in actual Lake Michigan shallows with a crew of eight, the film's holographic presentation is deliberately imperfect, with visible seams and depth errors that the director, Kwame Johansson-Patel, has described as 'the honest texture of a world that doesn't render cleanly for people like us.'
cultural_impact: Became a cult staple on pirate holographic projectors throughout Shelf communities, and the salvage diver protagonist is widely used as an avatar in Shelf mesh culture — representing anyone who finds something they weren't supposed to find.
story_hooks: The friend whose discovery inspired the film has resurfaced — literally, found floating in the lake — and left a dead drop for Johansson-Patel that the director is too frightened to retrieve alone.

The pre-Compact archive in the film is real, and at least two corponations are running parallel operations to locate and claim it before the other, creating a window for a third party to get there first.
A Tier 4 collector has paid Φ200,000 for a copy of the film — not to watch it, but because they believe Johansson-Patel encoded the archive's actual coordinates into the holographic depth-map data.
